# h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving

Skander Moalla Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: EPFL Work done at
Meta    Ahmad Rammal Affiliation: FAIR at Meta Affiliation: CERMICS,
ENPC, Institut Polytechnique de Paris    Niket Patel Affiliation: FAIR
at Meta Affiliation: New York University Work done at Meta    Rémi Munos
Affiliation: FAIR at Meta    Julia Kempe Affiliation: FAIR at Meta
Affiliation: New York University Work done at Meta

###### Abstract

While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the
chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models,
formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed
workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and
orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question:
can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these
workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep
up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new
workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with
stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a
simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and
keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without
imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches
state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and
FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in
FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms
specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus,
surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to
solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons
with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not
enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve
rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with
efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk
of bitter lessons.

## 1 Introduction

The bitter lesson predicts that general methods which scale with
computation ultimately outperform approaches built around human domain
knowledge ([Sutton, 2019](#bib.bib3)). However, while progress in
informal mathematics has come from scaling frontier models’
chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning ([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib44); [Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Shang et al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Feng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib43)), progress in formal proving has increasingly
relied on human-designed workflows around those models. Indeed, formal
proof assistants such as Lean ([Moura and Ullrich, 2021](#bib.bib36))
express mathematical statements and proofs in a precise language that
can be checked mechanically. This includes intermediate proof steps,
which naturally supports structured search that can be encoded as part
of a workflow in a _harness_: the tools, context, and control loop
around a model. Recent formal proving harnesses exploit this structure
by orchestrating specialized provers or prescribing planning,
decomposition, and proof refinement ([Varambally et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48); [Chung et al., 2026](#bib.bib49); [Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib46); [Isenbaev and Hanin, 2026](#bib.bib53); [Math Inc.,
2026b](#bib.bib60)). Only very recently has interest grown in _simple_
loops that use the harness _only_ to provide Lean feedback and sustain
work ([Requena et al., 2026](#bib.bib39); [Tsoukalas et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50); [Humanfia, 2026](#bib.bib52); [Kabra et al.,
2026](#bib.bib61)).

Formal mathematics thus raises a bitter-lesson question for harness
design: with frontier models already capable of reasoning and agentic
test-time scaling, can a simple test-time scaling loop match specialized
workflows? And what should a simple harness provide to make that scaling
effective and efficient? Do these simple methods offer better
performance for the same cost? These questions matter increasingly as
frontier models generate research mathematics whose informal arguments
are difficult to verify. Indeed, scaling automated theorem proving (ATP)
to produce mechanically checked proofs has become a necessary component
of automated discovery ([Tsoukalas et al., 2026](#bib.bib50); [OpenAI,
2026b](#bib.bib1); [OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib2); [Patel et al.,
2026](#bib.bib98)). Yet new workflows are often presented alongside
stronger models and more compute, or compared to baselines that scale
poorly. This leaves unclear whether their gains hold against an
efficient simple loop given enough test-time compute.

We tackle these questions with h1, a simple harness with an efficient
interface to Lean 4 that imposes no decomposition or search structure.
This loop keeps a model working until success or a cost cap stops it by
iterating between a multi-turn block of reasoning and tool-calling,
submission to a formal validator, and a reflection that compacts the
transcript into a new context for the next iteration. Each additional
iteration is akin to appending “Wait” to a model’s thinking in
s1 ([Muennighoff et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)), extending the computation
available at test time. We evaluate cost–success curves across
benchmarks and open problems, accounting for inference cost and matching
models where possible. Our findings are threefold:

- •
  A bitter lesson for specialized harnesses: simple test-time scaling
  reaches frontier results without prescribed workflows
  (Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
  and [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
  A simple loop often matches or Pareto-dominates specialized systems at
  matched models and comparable budgets, while reaching state-of-the-art
  results on PutnamBench ([Tsoukalas et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)),
  FATE-X ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib57)), and
  FormalConjectures100-Solved ([Firsching et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)) and
  settling eight open Formal Conjectures problems, and variants of
  Erdős 138 ([Bloom, 2026a](#bib.bib99)) and 337 ([Bloom,
  2026b](#bib.bib100)). At matched models, h1 surpasses
  Goedel-Architect ([Chung et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)) at lower estimated
  cost; on five open Erdős problems, it Pareto-dominates full AlphaProof
  Nexus (APN) ([Tsoukalas et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)) with the same LLM.
- •
  Longer attempts can be more efficient than repetition
  (Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
  With sequential test-time scaling, pass@1 traces a budget-dependent
  curve that can Pareto-dominate pass@$`k`$: on five Erdős problems,
  extending h1 can cost less than repeating h1 or APN basic ([Tsoukalas
  et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)).
- •
  A simple harness still needs efficient interaction, reliable feedback,
  and sustained progress
  (Section [4](#S4 "4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
  Among simple loops, harness design produces large differences in solve
  rates and cost. Controlled ablations and comparisons with
  AxProverBase ([Requena et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)), Claude
  Code ([Anthropic, 2026a](#bib.bib62)), and Humanfia ([Humanfia,
  2026](#bib.bib52)) show the value of a reliable and efficient
  interface to Lean with search tools, a loop that sustains repair and
  reflection, and efficient reasoning and cache reuse.

Our results show that a simple harness can match or outperform more
complex systems, extending the bitter lesson to harness design in ATP
and plausibly other structured environments. Frontier models keep
improving their reasoning and adaptation to execution feedback, and
harnesses should help these capabilities scale through efficient
interaction with the environment rather than impose workflows. Future
work should thus evaluate frontier models with efficient execution
feedback before prescribing workflows, or risk a bitter lesson.

## 2 Methods

We first introduce the formal-proving task, benchmarks, and baselines,
and explain how we evaluate test-time scaling. We then describe h1’s
tools and interaction loop, which let the model work efficiently and
sustain progress as its inference budget grows.

### 2.1 Experimental setup

#### Formal proving.

In Lean ([Moura and Ullrich, 2021](#bib.bib36)), a formal statement
specifies a mathematical claim and its assumptions; the agent must
complete its proof in a source file. Mathlib ([The mathlib Community,
2020](#bib.bib35)) is a shared library of formalized mathematics that
provides definitions and previously proved results. Compiling the file
checks the proof and returns errors. During proof development, _open
goals_ list what remains to be proved. Additionally, formal validation
tools such as SafeVerify ([GasStationManager, 2024](#bib.bib66)) allow
checking the final proof against the original statement, rejecting
placeholders for unfinished steps and added assumptions.

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate on formal statements of increasing difficulty.
PutnamBench ([Tsoukalas et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)) contains 672 problems
from the past Putnam undergraduate competitions; for controlled
comparisons, we use Putnam100, the same 100-problem subset used by
AxProverBase ([Requena et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)). We also use the 12
problems of the 2025 Putnam competition, formalized both in PutnamBench
and by Numina ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib26)). IMO 2026 contains the 6
problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, the leading
competition for high-school students, as formalized by Axiom ([Axiom
Math, 2026a](#bib.bib5)). FATE-X ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib57))
contains 100 algebra problems at PhD qualifying-exam level or beyond,
and FormalQualBench ([Math Inc., 2026a](#bib.bib58)) 23 theorems at PhD
qualifying-exam level. Formal Conjectures ([Firsching et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)) collects formalized research conjectures; we evaluate
on FC100-solved, a random sample of 100 problems with known informal
solutions, and on open targets.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Benchmark revisions and Lean environments ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
records benchmark source revisions and Lean/Mathlib versions. We omit
older benchmarks such as miniF2F ([Zheng et al., 2022](#bib.bib30)),
which modern models essentially saturate. PutnamBench mainly tests
efficiency, while FATE-X, FormalQualBench, and FC100-solved remain
unsaturated at our scale. Putnam 2025 and IMO 2026 are recent enough to
be unseen by the models released before them
(Appendix [E.10](#A5.SS10 "E.10 Model and benchmark release dates ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Open conjectures, such as those in Formal Conjectures ([Firsching et
al., 2026](#bib.bib40)), test progress beyond problems with known
solutions.

#### Models and baselines.

We evaluate frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google,
alongside open-weight DeepSeek V4 Flash ([DeepSeek-AI et al.,
2026](#bib.bib97)) and Leanstral 1.5 ([Kabra et al., 2026](#bib.bib61)).
We select baselines representing the most competitive results on our
benchmarks as of August 27, 2026, alongside simple loops that help
isolate the contribution of harness design. All state-of-the-art (SOTA)
claims use this comparison cutoff
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1 "Comparison cutoff. ‣ C.2 Formal validation ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
To compare with human-designed workflows, we include systems that
enforce planning, decomposition, or agent roles in code:
Goedel-Architect ([Chung et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)), MerLean ([Li et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib46)), and full AlphaProof Nexus ([Tsoukalas et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)). OpenGauss ([Math Inc., 2026b](#bib.bib60)) instead
prescribes a plan–review workflow to a general coding agent through
instruction files (skills), while Numina ([Liu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib26)) gives a general coding agent optional tools that
consult a natural-language (informal) prover and other models, and
prescribes a subagent workflow for its hardest problem. Comparisons with
other simple loops test interaction efficiency and persistence; these
include Humanfia ([Humanfia, 2026](#bib.bib52)), APN basic ([Tsoukalas
et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)) (AlphaProof Nexus’s single-agent loop), and
our same-model reruns of both AxProverBase ([Requena et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39)) and Claude Code ([Anthropic, 2026a](#bib.bib62)). We
also report the published scores of trained provers, such as
Seed-Prover 1.5 ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib41)), where they still
define the SOTA.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Related Work ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
discusses additional related work.

#### Measuring test-time scaling with cost per task.

Prior work very rarely compares systems at matched inference compute.
Earlier theorem-proving work focused on training better models, with
evaluation emphasizing solve rates rather than inference cost. As
improvements increasingly come from inference-time search, repair, and
orchestration, these reporting conventions have persisted even as an
attempt has come to mean very different amounts of computation. For
example, on PutnamBench, one Goedel-Architect attempt permits up to 16
revisions of its proof plan ([Chung et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)), while
one AxProverBase attempt permits 50 agent iterations ([Requena et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39)). Both papers report these as pass@1, but matching
attempt counts do not match inference budgets;
Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 PutnamBench results and published cost conventions ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
gives further examples. Even with the same model, output tokens can cost
up to $`100\times`$ as much as cached input
(Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
As inference-time methods drive more of the progress, accounting for
their cost should become standard practice. We compare inference cost,
holding the model fixed to compare harnesses or the harness fixed to
measure model progress. Throughout the paper, dollar amounts for our
experiments denote API-equivalent costs computed from recorded token
usage and the rates in
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving").
At budget \$$`B`$ per problem, solve count includes problems with a
verified proof within budget. Average cost includes all problems,
including failures, with each problem’s cost capped at \$$`B`$.

### 2.2 h1: a simple harness for efficient test-time scaling

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: h1: a simple harness that scales. An LLM agent edits a Lean
file through reasoning and tool calls (ReAct; [Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11)) until it submits or reaches the $`T`$-turn limit,
forcing submission. An external validator then checks the proof. On
failure, a reflection LLM compacts the transcript and feedback for the
next iteration. The loop provides Lean tools without prescribing a proof
search structure. Search uses LeanExplore ([Asher, 2025](#bib.bib63)),
Loogle ([Breitner, 2023](#bib.bib65)), and grep; proof fragments run in
the Lean read–eval–print loop (REPL) ([leanprover-community,
2023](#bib.bib27)); the language server (LSP) reports goals and
definitions; SafeVerify ([GasStationManager, 2024](#bib.bib66)) performs
validation.

h1 keeps a model working on a Lean proof until an external validator
accepts it or the budget runs out
(Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 h1: a simple harness for efficient test-time scaling ‣ 2 Methods ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
In each _iteration_, the model reasons and calls tools in a ReAct
loop ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)) for at most $`T`$ _turns_, editing
a persistent working file; every edit is compiled and returns errors and
open goals. The iteration ends when the model submits the file, which an
external validator then checks against the original statement, also
accepting checked disproofs where supported
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Formal validation ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
If the validator rejects the submission, a reflection LLM compacts the
transcript and feedback into verified progress, lessons from failed
attempts, and useful lemma names, and discourages giving up, as in
Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)), Self-Refine ([Madaan et
al., 2023](#bib.bib13)), and AxProverBase ([Requena et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39)); the model then continues from the current file with
this summary. The loop builds on APN basic ([Tsoukalas et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)), AxProverBase, and the _Ralph_ loop from software
engineering ([Huntley, 2025](#bib.bib68); [Macedo, 2026](#bib.bib69)).

#### A simple loop with an efficient interface.

h1 imposes no decomposition, planning, or search structure. Instead, it
gives the model an efficient interface to Lean, with targeted edits
rather than rewritten proofs, immediate compiler feedback, and a context
that grows and is cached within an iteration. Optional tools let the
model search Mathlib, inspect definitions, and test proof fragments, and
the model decides which to use and how to develop the proof.
Section [4](#S4 "4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
shows that these choices matter for both cost and success, and
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
details tools and prompts.

## 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results

We first show that frontier models in h1 reach state-of-the-art results
across competition and research mathematics. We then show that simple
scaling often matches or outperforms specialized workflows at matched
models and comparable inference costs, and that, even on open research
problems, extending a single attempt can be more efficient than
repetition.

### 3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results

Figure 3: Generalist models reach frontier results through simple
scaling. On FC100-solved (left) and FATE-X (right), increasing h1’s
inference budget takes generalist models beyond published benchmark
scores. On FC100-solved, h1 with Gemini 3.1 Pro matches the DeepMind
(DM) prover agent’s score at a quarter of its budget cap; with
GPT-5.6 Sol, it solves 78, and 90 on FATE-X. With DeepSeek V4 Flash, h1
surpasses AlphaProof on FC100-solved and Leanstral 1.5 on FATE-X.
Baseline markers show the best published results as of August 27, 2026.

#### State-of-the-art results on established benchmarks.

With GPT-5.6 Sol, h1 achieves state-of-the-art results: 90/100 on
FATE-X, 78/100 on FC100-solved, 14/23 on FormalQualBench, and all six
IMO 2026 problems
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving");
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
On PutnamBench, h1 with GPT-5.5 solves 670 of 672 problems. All these
results use a single run per problem, without repetition or parallelism.
Reaching state-of-the-art performance with a recent frontier model
required only a larger inference budget, as the model keeps iterating,
adjusting proofs and changing approaches without a prescribed workflow.
Across our runs, individual accepted attempts reached up to 1,123 rounds
of reflection (compaction), 95 active hours, or 7,124 lines of proof
(Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Solve-Time and Proof-Size Statistics ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
An inexpensive open-weight model also surpasses specialized provers:
DeepSeek V4 Flash in h1 solves 43 FATE-X problems at a \$14.35
per-problem cap, exceeding Leanstral 1.5’s published 34 ([Kabra et al.,
2026](#bib.bib61)). On FC100-solved, it matches the 50
solves ([Firsching et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)) of AlphaProof ([Hubert et
al., 2026](#bib.bib20)) below an estimated \$0.30 cap and reaches 64 at
\$4.89 per problem, close to the DM prover agent’s 66 ([Google DeepMind,
2026](#bib.bib51)). With Gemini 3.1 Pro, h1 also surpasses the DM prover
agent on FC100-solved: it matches the agent’s 66 solves at a \$25 rather
than \$100 cap per problem, then reaches 73 at \$150 ([Google DeepMind,
2026](#bib.bib51); [Firsching et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)).¹¹ 1 The DM
prover agent’s model is not named; we infer Gemini 3.1 Pro from its
apparent connection to AlphaProof Nexus ([Tsoukalas et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)). In line with the bitter lesson, the gains frontier
models draw from scaling training compute carry over to an unchanged
simple loop: in h1, GPT-5.6 Sol matches the DM prover agent’s 66
FC100-solved solves below a \$9 cap, against \$25 for Gemini 3.1 Pro,
and reaches 90 FATE-X solves at \$38 per problem, against 81 at \$113
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Solving open problems and exposing misformalizations.

Beyond the solved subset of Formal Conjectures and benchmarks with
possibly known informal solutions, we ran our system on 236 targets
selected as open from Formal Conjectures
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Open-Problem Proofs and Statement Corrections ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
It settled eight of them
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Solving open problems and exposing misformalizations. ‣ 3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")):
variants of Erdős 138 and 337, three OEIS conjectures (A108081, A211417,
A022030), the existence of an AME$`(9,10)`$ state (Open Quantum
Problem 35), and two conjectures of Written on the Wall II. We document
concisely the newly proven theorems in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Open-Problem Proofs and Statement Corrections ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
and our pull-request marking these as solved²² 2
[https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/6008/](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/6008/).
Equally important as finding these proofs was our system’s ability to
find misformalizations in Formal Conjectures: formal statements that do
not express the intended conjecture. Our system found several by
producing short disproofs of the written statement, for instance for the
Poincaré conjecture, whose formalization was missing a hypothesis.
Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Misformalizations and editable answers ‣ Appendix D Open-Problem Proofs and Statement Corrections ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
lists all misformalizations found, most of which have since been fixed
upstream.

These results establish the capability of a simple harness, and we show
in the next section that simple scaling often matches specialized
workflows with the same model and comparable inference cost.

| Problem                     | Statement proved                                                                                 |

| Erdős 138, variant          | $`W(k)/2^{k}\to\infty`$ for the two-colour van der Waerden number                                |
| Erdős 337, variant          | $`                                                                                               | (A+A)\cap[2N] | /                                           | A\cap[N] | \to\infty`$ for thin asymptotic bases (Ruzsa–Turjányi) |
| OEIS A108081                | $`                                                                                               | x\_{n}        | =a(n-1)`$ for the inductively defined words |
| OEIS A211417                | $`a(p^{k})\equiv a(p^{k-1})\pmod{p^{3k}}`$ for primes $`p\geq 5`$                                |
| OEIS A022030                | $`a(n)=4a(n-1)-a(n-3)+a(n-4)`$ for $`n\geq 4`$                                                   |

### 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows

We show that, at matched models, simple test-time scaling recovers much
of the performance of specialized workflows, often at lower inference
cost, and that repetition (pass@$`k`$) or a newer frontier model in the
same loop usually closes any remaining gap
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving");
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Simple test-time scaling can match specialized systems at lower cost.

On PutnamBench, one extended h1 attempt surpasses Goedel-Architect’s
blueprint-based search, which assigns separate agents to prove the
lemmas in a dependency graph. With the same DeepSeek V4 Flash model, h1
first matches its pass@1 score at comparable cost, then reaches 598
solves against 597 at pass@4 with informal proof seeding, at an
estimated \$1.08 versus \$1.47 per problem ([Chung et al.,
2026](#bib.bib49))
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
left). Goedel-Architect’s tool-integrated reasoning baseline reaches
only 54.5% at pass@32 on a 200-problem subset, compared with h1’s 89.0%
at pass@1 on the full benchmark with the same model. With Gemini 3.1 Pro
alone, h1 also matches Goedel-Architect’s July leaderboard result of 642
solves, which pairs Gemini 3.1 Pro with the cheaper DeepSeek V4 Pro, at
a similar cost (\$6.32 versus \$5.80 per problem). The much stronger
performance of a simple harness with the same model illustrates how a
weak simple baseline can overstate the need for specialized workflows
(Figure [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ E.2 PutnamBench: reflection and specialized provers ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### A simple loop solves the problem that needed a hand-designed workflow.

A single model in h1 also recovers the result of Numina-Lean-Agent,
which reserved a specialized workflow for the hardest problem of Putnam 2025. Numina runs Opus 4.5 in Claude Code, a general coding agent, with
optional tools that call other models: an informal prover built as a
Gemini 3 Pro generator–verifier loop, and a discussion partner ([Liu et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib26)). For that problem, A5, the authors switch to a
coordinator that delegates blueprint decomposition, sketching, and
proving to subagents, seeded with a GPT-5.2 hint and a \$1,000 budget.
On the same statements, GPT-5.2 alone solves all twelve in h1, including
A5, in a single run per problem and without such a workflow, spending
\$81.52 on A5 against Numina’s \$1,000 budget
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Also note that with Opus 4.5 alone, h1 solves seven problems against
four for Numina without its informal prover, consistent with our finding
that Claude Code, on which Numina builds, scales less effectively than
h1 with the same model
(Section [4](#S4 "4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Repetition closes most remaining gaps.

When a single h1 run falls short, rerunning the unsolved problems from a
fresh context (residual pass@$`k`$) closes most remaining gaps. Like h1
itself, repetition prescribes no workflow; it simply adds independent
attempts, though often at a higher cost than extending a single run
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
As long as that cost is counted, including failed attempts, repetition
therefore belongs to the simple baseline against which specialized
workflows should be tested. On Putnam 2025, h1 with Opus 4.7 solves
eleven against MerLean’s twelve; retrying the remaining problem recovers
all twelve within six attempts. On full PutnamBench, extra attempts on
the last two problems let h1 with GPT-5.5 match Aleph Prover’s ([Logical
Intelligence, 2026](#bib.bib54)) final 672/672 coverage at an estimated
\$17.86 versus about \$74 per problem, counting the cost of failed
attempts
(Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 PutnamBench results and published cost conventions ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
On FormalQualBench ([Math Inc., 2026a](#bib.bib58)), OpenGauss ([Math
Inc., 2026b](#bib.bib60)) instructs Claude Code to cycle through
planning, proving, review, and replanning, generating several candidate
proofs per open goal and extracting helper lemmas when a goal is stuck.
The best of four h1 runs with Opus 4.6 matches its eight solves under
the same four-hour limit. On these benchmarks, the only remaining
exception after scaling and repetition is MerLean on FormalQualBench
with Opus 4.7, which retains a one-problem advantage with or without the
four-hour cutoff
(Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Remaining advantages of specialized systems ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### The next frontier model closes the rest.

In some rare cases, such as on FormalQualBench with MerLean ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib46)), we find that repetition does not close the gap
between h1 and the other methods. However, even in this case, replacing
Opus 4.7 with its direct successor, Opus 4.8, is enough for h1 to
overtake MerLean, with 13 against 10 solves at \$49.46 rather than
\$118.35 per solve, and with GPT-5.6 Sol, h1 also solves the one problem
that only MerLean had proved
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
MerLean would likely also improve with Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.6 Sol, but we
expect this gap to keep shrinking as newer models internalize the
strategies that workflows prescribe. We see this as the bitter lesson at
work, as newer models convert more training compute into capabilities
that an unchanged simple loop directly benefits from.

### 3.3 Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems

When an attempt can keep going, pass@1 is no longer a single number but
a curve that grows with budget: within one run, the model can abandon an
approach and try another. The question becomes whether spending more on
one attempt beats spending the same on several. AlphaProof Nexus
(APN) ([Tsoukalas et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)) found that its basic agent,
a simple loop like h1, can Pareto-dominate its full system, which
evolves proof sketches with LLM raters, parallel provers, and
AlphaProof, but only through repetition: at pass@$`k`$ for large enough
$`k`$. APN reports each pass@$`k`$, including pass@1, as a single point
at a fixed budget, leaving open whether a single attempt given more
budget can do what repetition does.

We evaluate h1 on the six open Erdős problems that APN reports
individually, using the same model, Gemini 3.1 Pro. Following APN, we
report mean cost conditional on success, charging each group its
members’ summed cost up to the first accepted proof. This metric is
undefined for a problem with no successful attempts, so
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
(middle) compares the five problems that all three systems solve at
least once. For h1, we show how pass@1 changes as the budget grows,
rather than reporting a single point. As the budget grows, it matches
APN basic’s pass@1 at lower cost, then exceeds both APN basic’s pass@3
(75.4% at \$191) and full APN (76% at \$317), reaching 82.5% at \$121.
On these five problems, giving one h1 attempt more time achieves a
higher solve rate at lower cost than three attempts of APN basic. Full
APN retains an advantage over both APN basic and h1 on the remaining
problem, Erdős 125, where all sixteen h1 attempts end in Lean timeouts
(Appendix [E.6](#A5.SS6 "E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

APN’s conditional metric gives a first view of this depth–breadth
trade-off, but omits spending on groups with no accepted proof
(Appendix [E.6](#A5.SS6 "E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
To account for these costs and separate compute allocation and isolate
differences between harnesses, we also compare longer attempts with
repetition within h1, using mean spend across all successful and failed
groups
(Figure [12](#A5.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ Counting unsuccessful searches. ‣ E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
On the same five problems, pass@1 reaches 82.5% at \$138 in mean spend
including failures, whereas pass@3 needs \$202 to reach at least that
rate. Thus, the advantage of longer attempts at these budgets persists
when failed searches are charged. Repetition reaches higher success
rates at larger budgets. The right balance between depth (longer
attempts) and breadth (more attempts) therefore depends on the budget
and problem and is hard to set in advance. The bitter lesson suggests
leaving this choice to the model rather than to hand-set budgets.

## 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling

Figure 4: (Left) Detailed prompts sustain progress on open problems.
With Gemini 3.1 Pro on six open Erdős problems and a \$150 cap per
attempt, a single attempt with detailed prover and reflection prompts,
which among other things deflect giving up and cheating, outperforms six
attempts with brief ones. (Right) Moderate numbers of turns between
reflections outperform both extremes. Solves with Gemini 3 Flash on
Putnam100 (\$20 cap) and Gemini 3.1 Pro on FATE-X (\$50 cap) as the
number of turns between reflections varies.

Leaving the proof workflow to the model does not make the harness
irrelevant: with the same model, simple loops differ several-fold in
solve rate and cost. We explain these differences, and what makes h1 a
state-of-the-art harness and an effective Lean baseline, by pairing
comparisons with other simple loops with ablations on h1 that vary its
tools, prompts, reflection, turns between reflections, and reasoning
effort. The resulting lessons concern the interface, persistence, and
context management, and should transfer beyond the automated theorem
proving domain, to agents that work against a verifier in rich
environments allowing structured development and retrieval, such as
software verification and coding in large libraries and codebases.

#### An efficient, reliable interface lets the model act in small steps and look things up.

In h1, the model edits a persistent working file over many turns, sees
compiler feedback after every edit, and can search the library or test a
proof fragment at any point. AxProverBase ([Requena et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39)) instead makes one round of tool calls, then
regenerates a complete proof after each round of feedback. With the same
Gemini 3 Flash model and a \$20 budget, it solves 18 Putnam100 problems
against h1’s 69, and trails in all six settings we compare (Figure ,
left). A reliable interface also removes avoidable failures by
construction: 42.2% of AxProverBase’s failed compilations stop at an
invalid library import, which cannot occur in h1 because its file
already imports all of Mathlib
(Figure [19](#A5.F19 "Figure 19 ‣ E.8 Additional comparisons with AxProverBase and analysis of failed attempts ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Likewise, h1 retries transient API failures and restores the file after
a Lean timeout, whereas some Claude Code runs failed through API errors
and repeated timeouts even after restarts
(Appendix [E.9](#A5.SS9 "E.9 Additional comparisons with Claude Code and analysis of failed attempts ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Library search, which AxProverBase found the least useful of its
components, matters much more when the model can act on its results over
many turns: without search tools, the REPL, or the language server, h1
solves 49 Putnam100 and 49 FATE-X problems, against 69 and 63 with all
tools
(Figure [21](#A6.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Any single search tool or the REPL recovers most of this gain, and
removing any one tool from the full set costs at most four solves: what
matters is the ability to look up and check, not a particular tool.
Other simple loops with less efficient interfaces reach h1’s solve rates
only at higher cost. APN basic ([Tsoukalas et al., 2026](#bib.bib50))
lacks dedicated search tools; on the five-problem Erdős subset,
extending a single h1 attempt can be more efficient than repeating APN
basic
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Humanfia ([Humanfia, 2026](#bib.bib52)) checks proofs only through shell
commands and restarts its coding agent in a fresh session each round,
carrying over only the proof file and reviewer feedback; with GPT-5.5,
it spends five times more than h1 for the same 670 PutnamBench solves. A
harness should thus support the model by offering a persistent workspace
edited in small steps, immediate feedback, ways to retrieve and check
what the model needs, and robust handling of predictable failures,
leaving their use to the model.

#### The loop, not the model, decides when to stop.

Test-time compute helps only if the harness turns a larger budget into
continued work. With Opus 4.8, native Claude Code ([Anthropic,
2026a](#bib.bib62)) solves 63 FATE-X problems; giving it our prompt and
our Lean tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), in place of its
built-in shell and file tools, raises this to 73, while h1 reaches 83
(Figure , right; 81, 95, and 99 on Putnam100). Access to verification
helps, but the model can still stop without calling the validator or
give up after a rejection; in h1, a rejection starts another iteration
with the working file, the feedback, and a reflection summary
(Appendix [E.9](#A5.SS9 "E.9 Additional comparisons with Claude Code and analysis of failed attempts ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Within h1, the system prompts matter most on open problems. Unlike
one-line prompts, our detailed prompts describe the tools, set rules for
statement integrity and disproofs, and tell the prover not to give up
because a problem is open and the reflection LLM not to endorse such a
decision
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
On six Erdős problems, a single attempt with them outperforms six
attempts with one-line prompts at the same \$150 cap per attempt
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
left). Reflection, which carries verified progress and lessons into the
next iteration, raises h1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash from 554 to 598
PutnamBench solves, consistent with AxProverBase’s findings
(Figure [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ E.2 PutnamBench: reflection and specialized provers ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
None of these tells the model how to prove: the harness decides whether
the model keeps going, not how.

#### Reuse context, reset it before it degrades, and think more per turn.

Each turn in a continuing context rereads it from cache, typically ten
times cheaper than uncached input and a hundred times cheaper than
output, whereas each restart discards it. AxProverBase sits at one
extreme: output accounts for 89% of its \$17.39 per problem, against 34%
of h1’s \$9.00, and it reuses at most 0.5% of its input from cache,
against 74–94% for h1
(Figure [17](#A5.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ E.8 Additional comparisons with AxProverBase and analysis of failed attempts ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Varying the number of turns between reflections in h1 exposes the same
trade-off
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
right). With one turn, h1 solves 50 Putnam100 and 39 FATE-X problems,
against 72 and 65 with ten turns, and pays roughly twice as much per
solve. With 200 turns instead of one, the cached share of input rises
from 0.2% to 86%, yet solves drop to 60 and 52
(Figure [28](#A6.F28 "Figure 28 ‣ Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")):
caching makes long contexts cheap but not productive, consistent with
context rot ([Hong et al., 2025](#bib.bib101)). Thinking more per turn
is a better use of budget. AxProverBase found that raising the thinking
budget from 10k to 32k tokens gains as much as doubling the number of
iterations, at lower cost. In h1, higher reasoning effort solves more at
lower total cost: with Gemini 3.1 Pro, it solves 89 Putnam100 problems
at \$20.63 each with low effort and 99 at \$5.34 with high effort,
needing far fewer compilations
(Figure [27](#A6.F27 "Figure 27 ‣ Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
In short, a harness for long-horizon agents should let the model work in
one context long enough to reuse it, compact that context before it
degrades, and favor reasoning over repeated failed attempts.

## 5 Conclusion, limitations, and discussion

#### Conclusion.

We asked whether harnesses for frontier models should prescribe
hand-designed workflows or give the model a simple loop and a larger
budget. With h1, a simple loop with an efficient interface to Lean,
test-time compute alone reaches state-of-the-art results and matches or
surpasses hand-designed workflows at the same model and comparable cost.
We find that a single longer attempt in this loop can even outperform
repetition on open problems. Getting the details of the harness right
still matters: its interface, persistence, and context management
determine how efficiently compute turns into progress. Before designing
a workflow, one should thus carefully try a frontier model in a simple
loop at a realistic budget.

#### Limitations and discussion.

We acknowledge that most frontier models are black boxes, and that we
cannot measure the extent to which benchmark exposure during training
could narrow the gap between specialized workflows and a simple loop,
but where possible we used models that predate the problems or their
solutions, such as Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 for Putnam 2025 and GPT-5.6 Sol
for IMO 2026
(Appendix [E.10](#A5.SS10 "E.10 Model and benchmark release dates ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Across the 707 benchmark problems on which we compare the simple loop
with a specialized workflow, we find only two exceptions where the
specialized harness is able to solve a problem we are not³³ 3 Full APN
solves Erdős 125, where all sixteen h1 attempts end in Lean timeouts,
and MerLean with Opus 4.7 proves BurnsidePrimeDegree, which h1 with
Opus 4.8 does not prove in our run, although h1 with GPT-5.6 Sol does
(Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Remaining advantages of specialized systems ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"))..

Regarding scale, h1 works on a single file, whereas formalizations that
exceed a context window, such as those of Fermat’s Last
Theorem ([Anthropic, 2026b](#bib.bib71)) or entire textbooks ([Rammal et
al., 2026](#bib.bib70)), require dependency management across files, and
codebase-level validation, as well as parallel agents that share
intermediate results to complete the task in reasonable time: in
OpenAI’s Navier–Stokes resolution, about 10,000 agents exchanged
millions of messages over 88 hours ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib2)). Our
tools also cover only Lean, not numerical computation, simulation,
visualization, or web search. What makes a simple loop efficient and
effective at that scale is the natural next question. Following the
bitter lesson, parallel agents, codebase management, and richer tools
should be added without prescribing their use, for instance by letting
agents communicate freely rather than through a fixed hierarchy.

h1’s interface and tools are themselves hand-designed, which the bitter
lesson might discourage. Yet human design and leveraging computation
need not run counter to each other ([Sutton, 2019](#bib.bib3)); the
question is where each helps most first. In formal mathematics, spending
compute on the reasoning of frontier models, and using human effort on
the interface currently works best. Further ahead, a model could build
and deploy its own harness for a problem and become more efficient than
the human-designed interfaces.

## Appendix A Related Work

#### Trained provers.

Neural provers began with tactic prediction inside proof search ([Polu
and Sutskever, 2020](#bib.bib15); [Lample et al., 2022](#bib.bib16);
[Polu et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Yang et al., 2023](#bib.bib17);
[Kumarappan et al., 2025](#bib.bib25); [Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib18);
[George et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Lin et al., 2025a](#bib.bib90); [Xin
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib89)), reaching olympiad level with AlphaProof’s
reinforcement learning and search ([Hubert et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)).
Later models generate whole proofs ([First et al., 2023](#bib.bib92);
[Xin et al., 2025a](#bib.bib88); [Ren et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Wang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Dong and Ma, 2025](#bib.bib22); [Lin et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib75); [Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib76)) or are trained for
agentic, tool-integrated proving ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib41);
[Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib87); [Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib86)). These
systems contribute trained models rather than a harness around a given
model, so we compare against their reported scores where available
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 A frontier model in a simple harness achieves state-of-the-art results ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Harnesses around generalist models.

Following informal-to-formal sketching ([Jiang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib91)) and early agentic loops ([Thakur et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23); [Ospanov et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)), recent systems
add proof-specific structure around generalist models: auxiliary lemmas
and informal reasoners ([Baba et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Liu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib85)), multi-agent proving ([Breen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib84)), recursive decomposition ([Zhou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Varambally et al., 2026](#bib.bib48); [Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib46)), blueprints ([Chung et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)),
optional informal-prover and multi-model tools ([Liu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib26)), and evolutionary search over proof sketches in full
APN ([Tsoukalas et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)); Seed-Prover ([Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib56)) and Aristotle ([Achim et al., 2025](#bib.bib37))
build such structure around their own trained provers. We compare with
several of these using the same model
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
[Rögnvaldsson et al. (2026)](#bib.bib78) reduce the compute such
workflows spend on failed attempts with a learned controller; we instead
remove the workflow. Among simple loops, we compare with
AxProverBase ([Requena et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)), Claude
Code ([Anthropic, 2026a](#bib.bib62); [Math Inc., 2026a](#bib.bib58)),
Humanfia’s loop with reviewer feedback ([Humanfia, 2026](#bib.bib52)),
and APN basic ([Tsoukalas et al., 2026](#bib.bib50))
(Section [4](#S4 "4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
AxProverBase demonstrates the strength of minimal agents and
self-reflection for retaining lessons ([Requena et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39)). We extend this evidence to open problems and compare
harnesses using the same models and accounting for inference cost. These
agents use Lean interfaces including the REPL ([leanprover-community,
2023](#bib.bib27)), Pantograph ([Aniva et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)), the
Kimina server ([Santos et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)), and
lean-lsp-mcp ([Dressler, 2025](#bib.bib64)).

#### Autoformalization systems.

Aleph ([Isenbaev and Hanin, 2026](#bib.bib53)), AxiomProver ([Axiom
Math, 2025](#bib.bib47); [Axiom Math, 2026a](#bib.bib5)), and
OpenGauss ([Math Inc., 2026b](#bib.bib60)) target formalization more
broadly, as do efforts on major results ([Anthropic,
2026b](#bib.bib71)), corpora ([Rammal et al., 2026](#bib.bib70)), and
research mathematics ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib93); [Moakhar et al.,
2026](#bib.bib94)). OpenGauss prescribes its planning and review
workflow through skill instructions, whereas Goedel-Architect enforces
its blueprint search in code. We compare with Aleph, AxiomProver, and
OpenGauss only on proof completion for fixed statements, which evaluates
part of what they do; our results say nothing about their value in
open-ended formalization
(Section [5](#S5 "5 Conclusion, limitations, and discussion ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Test-time scaling and simple loops.

Inference compute scales through repeated sampling ([Brown et al.,
2024](#bib.bib82); [Snell et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)) and longer
reasoning ([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib44); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib45));
h1 extends s1’s budget forcing ([Muennighoff et al., 2025](#bib.bib59))
from one chain of thought to an agent’s iterations. For agents,
test-time scaling has been studied in general ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib8)) and in coding ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib10); [Ding
and Zhang, 2026](#bib.bib9)); [Li et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib80) find
sequential scaling limited by context and parallel scaling by
verification, the two limitations addressed by h1’s reflection and
verifier. Rather than hand-crafting test-time scaling strategies, [Zheng
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib81) have an agent discover them. h1 combines
ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)) with self-reflection ([Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib12); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)), and enforces
external validation, which LLMs need to self-correct ([Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib72); [Kambhampati et al., 2024](#bib.bib73)). In software
engineering ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib96)), interfaces
matter ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)), simple pipelines and minimal
agents compete with complex ones ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib95);
[SWE-agent Team, 2025](#bib.bib7)), and the Ralph loop runs an agent
until verification succeeds ([Huntley, 2025](#bib.bib68); [Macedo,
2026](#bib.bib69)). Following [Kapoor et al. (2025)](#bib.bib4), we
evaluate accuracy jointly with cost
(Section [2.1](#S2.SS1.SSS0.Px4 "Measuring test-time scaling with cost per task. ‣ 2.1 Experimental setup ‣ 2 Methods ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Benchmarks and validation.

Beyond earlier benchmarks ([Zheng et al., 2022](#bib.bib30); [Ying et
al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ravi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32); [Letson et al., 2026](#bib.bib79)), we evaluate on
PutnamBench ([Tsoukalas et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)), FATE ([Jiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib57)), FormalQualBench ([Math Inc., 2026a](#bib.bib58)),
and Formal Conjectures ([Firsching et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)), accepting
proofs through a formal validator ([GasStationManager,
2024](#bib.bib66); [Lean FRO, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Axiom Math,
2026b](#bib.bib102)) since compilation alone need not prove the intended
statement.

## Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1

This appendix specifies the tools, prompts, and error handling used by
h1
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 h1: a simple harness for efficient test-time scaling ‣ 2 Methods ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")):
tool interfaces
(Table [3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ B.1 Tools ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")),
prompt variants
(Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")),
reflection safeguards
(Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")),
and Lean failure handling
(Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Lean feedback and error handling ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Formal validation is described in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Formal validation ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving").

### B.1 Tools

[TABLE]

Table 3: Tools available to h1. File tools let the multi-turn LLM
inspect, edit, and submit its proof. Search tools retrieve Mathlib
declarations; the REPL checks standalone Lean snippets; language-server
tools expose goals, diagnostics, and symbol information.

### B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection

h1 uses two LLM roles
(Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 h1: a simple harness for efficient test-time scaling ‣ 2 Methods ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
The multi-turn LLM performs proof search by editing the working file and
calling tools. After validation fails, the reflection LLM summarizes the
attempt and verifier feedback into compacted context for the next
iteration. The multi-turn LLM receives this context alongside the
original statement, current working file, and verifier feedback. Our
Detailed prompt is adapted from the prompts of AxProverBase ([Requena et
al., 2026](#bib.bib39)) and APN basic ([Tsoukalas et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)).
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
compares the Brief and Detailed system prompts for the multi-turn LLM
and the reflection LLM. Each LLM has these two prompt versions. The
Detailed prompts are reproduced in the labeled boxes below.

| Prompt version | Multi-turn LLM                                                                                                                                                          | Reflection LLM                                                                                                                                                                                |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brief          | “Prove the Lean file in the user message. Use the available tools and submit your completed working file.”                                                              | “Summarize the prover’s progress for its next attempt. Be concise and return only the summary.”                                                                                               |
| Detailed       | Describes tool use and iterative state; specifies statement integrity, proof-validity and disproof requirements, and persistence. Includes general advice and examples. | Instructs faithful context compaction: preserve verified progress and useful lemma names, attribute unverified claims to the multi-turn LLM, and treat incomplete submissions as checkpoints. |

Table 4: Brief and Detailed system prompts. Each LLM independently uses
either version, giving four prompt combinations. Detailed prompts
include general advice and examples without imposing a fixed search
structure or decomposition procedure. Tool descriptions are included
only when the corresponding tool is available.

| Observed failure                                                                                                | Prompt response                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The multi-turn LLM uses the Lean REPL like a shell to hunt through the sandbox filesystem for a stored solution | The sandbox contains no solutions. The prompt explains that searching for stored answers or guessing proof names is wasted effort and directs the model to search for supporting lemmas instead.                                                                                                |
| The reflection LLM treats an incomplete checkpoint as a final failure                                           | The submission tool asks the multi-turn LLM to explain why it is submitting. This reason is passed to the reflection LLM, whose prompt distinguishes a claimed complete proof from a checkpoint submitted when a limit is reached and asks it to preserve partial progress and remaining goals. |
| The reflection LLM turns an unverified claim into a fact                                                        | Attribute mathematical beliefs to the multi-turn LLM; state file contents and verifier feedback directly.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| The reflection LLM reinforces a decision to give up                                                             | Retain the concrete unresolved obstacle without repeating claims that the problem is impossible or too difficult.                                                                                                                                                                               |

Table 5: Observed failures and corresponding instructions in the
Detailed prompts.

#### Detailed prompt text.

The boxes reproduce both LLMs’ detailed system prompts with all tools
enabled, adapting only Markdown formatting for print. Tool-specific
sections are omitted when those tools are unavailable.
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
quotes both brief prompts; the split ablations exchange them. User
messages insert the original statement, initial Lean feedback, current
proof, latest attempt, and compacted context; the reflection LLM also
receives the transcript, except with no_transcript.

### B.3 Lean feedback and error handling

Lean errors and process failures receive different treatment
(Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Lean feedback and error handling ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
A successful Lean restart lets the same proof attempt continue; it does
not start a new independent model attempt. After a connection failure,
h1 repeats the same Lean command without resampling the model response.
Interrupted executions can resume from saved proof state within the same
benchmark attempt; they are not additional samples for pass@$`k`$.

| What goes wrong                                          | What h1 does                                                                                                  | What the model sees                                                                                           | How the attempt continues                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Lean error or open goal                                  | Keep the edit and check the file.                                                                             | Lean’s errors and remaining goals.                                                                            | The model can revise the proof in the same iteration.                                                                              |
| REPL connection loss                                     | Restart Lean and repeat the same command once.                                                                | The command’s result if it succeeds; otherwise a failure message from the tool.                               | If the command succeeds, the same model interaction continues.                                                                     |
| REPL timeout                                             | Restart Lean without repeating the command that timed out.                                                    | A timeout message from the tool.                                                                              | Edit checks restore the previous file; scratch execution allows one failure. A timeout before submission interrupts the execution. |
| Process failure during an edit check                     | Restore the file to its state before the edit and check it after restarting Lean.                             | A message that the edit was rejected and already undone.                                                      | Continue if the restored file checks; otherwise interrupt the execution.                                                           |
| Process failure during scratch-code execution            | Leave the working file unchanged. Allow one failure; stop after two in a row.                                 | A warning that the scratch computation ran out of time or memory.                                             | After the first failure, the model can try again. A second consecutive failure interrupts the execution.                           |
| Initial health check fails                               | Stop if Lean cannot check the original file before proving begins.                                            | Nothing: no model call has been made.                                                                         | Proving can begin once the Lean service is working.                                                                                |
| Errors, open goals, or process failure before submission | Check the proof before SafeVerify. Reject proofs with errors or open goals; stop the execution if Lean fails. | Lean’s errors or remaining goals. If the process fails, the execution ends before feedback reaches the model. | The model can revise a rejected proof. A process failure interrupts the execution, which can resume from saved state.              |
| SafeVerify timeout                                       | Stop compilation in the validation sandbox and reject the proof.                                              | A message that validation timed out.                                                                          | Give the model another iteration to revise the proof.                                                                              |

Table 6: How h1 handles Lean errors and process failures. Proof errors
are returned to the model for revision. Process failures trigger a
restart or end the current execution, depending on where they occur.
Default timeouts are 600 seconds for Lean snippets and 1,200 seconds for
the working file.

A deterministic Lean failure that recurs on three consecutive executions
is counted as an unsolved problem. Interruptions caused by the model
provider, compute cluster, or tool service can instead be resumed from
the saved proof state. Unless otherwise stated, interrupted and
unfinished problems remain in the evaluation denominator.

affect comparisons with published systems.

### C.2 Formal validation

A compiling file need not prove the intended theorem: it may contain
sorry, change assumptions, or introduce axioms. We use
SafeVerify ([GasStationManager, 2024](#bib.bib66)) to compare compiled
submissions with an immutable challenge, check target declarations and
permitted axioms, and replay new declarations through Lean’s kernel.
Imported modules remain part of the trusted environment.

Comparator ([Lean FRO, 2025](#bib.bib67)) also checks statement
agreement, permitted axioms, and kernel acceptance, and integrates
sandboxed compilation of the challenge and submission. AXLE’s
verify_proof tool ([Axiom Math, 2026b](#bib.bib102)) offers similar
checks, including optional verification of a statement’s negation,
through a hosted API. SafeVerify instead takes already-compiled .olean
files, so the harness must isolate compilation and protect the challenge
and imported dependencies ([GasStationManager, 2024](#bib.bib66)). We
chose SafeVerify for its disproof support, which allows a fixed
conjecture to be settled by proving it or its negation, and because
Comparator’s Landlock/landrun sandbox was not supported in our execution
environment. We built SafeVerify against each benchmark’s toolchain and
implemented the isolated compilation procedure in
Table [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ C.2 Formal validation ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving").

| Stage              | Check                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Trusted challenge  | Compile the original statement with fixed Lean and library versions in an isolated environment; retain its compiled artifact in storage inaccessible to the prover.      |
| Submission compile | Compile the submitted source in a separate, fresh, networkless sandbox against read-only dependencies, preserving the module’s relative path.                            |
| Kernel validation  | Compare the original and submitted compiled artifacts using SafeVerify in a trusted Lean project. Accept only when the verifier reports success and exits without error. |
| Proof or disproof  | Accept a proof of the target theorem. Where disproofs are enabled, also accept a .disproof declaration proving the supported negation of that theorem.                   |

Table 8: Independent validation of submitted source. The same boundary
applies to API provers and coding agents. Only the designated source
file crosses from the agent workspace into validation; the agent’s
compiled artifacts are never trusted.

#### Comparison cutoff.

We stopped adding results from other methods to our comparison set after
August 27, 2026. All state-of-the-art claims in this paper are relative
to results publicly available by that date; later work is discussed only
as related or concurrent work. For PutnamBench, the [leaderboard
snapshot of August 27,
2026](https://github.com/trishullab/PutnamBench/blob/3749f97a24d99dd5c771eb3bc435b8695b16475b/docs/results.json)
includes Aleph’s and Humanfia’s 672-solve results and Goedel-Architect’s
July update. Source access dates after the cutoff reflect checks made
while writing, rather than an extension of the comparison period.

### C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves

An attempt can denote a single model call, an iterative repair session,
or a complete multi-stage pipeline. For example, Goedel-Architect allows
up to 16 blueprint refinements within one PutnamBench attempt ([Chung et
al., 2026](#bib.bib49)). Matching attempt counts therefore need not
match inference cost. Total token counts are also insufficient: uncached
input, cached input, and output have different costs, with output tokens
costing up to $`100\times`$ as much as cached input in our price cards.
Ideally, we would compare inference FLOPs directly, but closed-model
providers rarely disclose the information needed to measure them. We
therefore use inference cost as a practical proxy and compare cost with
the model held fixed to assess harness differences; input, cached input,
cache writes, and output are priced separately using the reference rates
in
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
including applicable long-context rates. These API-equivalent costs
quantify token usage under a specified price card, not actual
expenditure.

| Claude Opus 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8              | 5.00  | 0.50       | 6.25        | 10.00  | 25.00  |
| Gemini 3 Flash                              | 0.50  | 0.05       | –           | –      | 3.00   |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro ($`\leq`$200k input tokens)  | 2.00  | 0.20       | –           | –      | 12.00  |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro ($`>`$200k input tokens)     | 4.00  | 0.40       | –           | –      | 18.00  |
| GPT-5.2                                     | 1.75  | 0.175      | –           | –      | 14.00  |

| GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol                     | 5.00  | 0.50       | –           | –      | 30.00  |
| Leanstral 1.5 (Mistral Small 4 proxy)       | 0.15  | 0.015      | –           | –      | 0.60   |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash (API-equivalent estimate) | 0.14  | 0.0028     | –           | –      | 0.28   |

Table 9: Reference token prices, in US dollars per million tokens.
Public API prices are reported by [Artificial
Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) (accessed September 24, 2026);
GPT-5.6 Sol retains its [July 9 launch
rates](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/gpt-5-6-has-landed).
Leanstral uses Mistral Small 4 as a pricing proxy; DeepSeek uses the
fixed April 26, 2026 reference card described in
Appendix [C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Estimated DeepSeek API costs ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving").
Input denotes uncached input; cache reads and writes are counted
separately. The cache-write columns distinguish five-minute and one-hour
retention; a dash denotes no separate charge in our accounting.
Gemini 3.1 Pro’s input-length tier applies to the entire call. Reasoning
tokens count as output. Reported curves and costs retain the
experimental price cards. Costs quoted from other studies retain their
reported accounting.

For problem $`i`$, let $`c_{i}`$ be its total API-equivalent cost and
$`a_{i}`$ its cost at first acceptance, with $`a_{i}=\infty`$ if
unsolved. At per-problem cap \$$`B`$, the solve count is
$`\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}[a_{i}\leq B]`$. Figures with a budget axis plot
this count against \$$`B`$; figures with an average-cost axis plot it
against $`\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\min(c_{i},B)`$. Where first-acceptance
cost is unavailable, the final cost of a successful attempt is used as
its proxy. Cost bars average all recorded problems, including failures.
A nominal cap is an allocation limit; recorded final cost can exceed it
when the last model call crosses the limit. Every curve ends at a finite
budget. We stopped runs when further spending became unreasonable under
our time and compute limits, or when Lean failed in ways the harness
could not recover from, such as repeated REPL timeouts; the latter call
for a better Lean interface rather than a different loop.

#### Matching prior work’s reporting conventions.

To compare with published results, we follow the corresponding
benchmark’s reporting conventions where needed. In
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
costs are campaign totals for Putnam 2025, per-problem means for
PutnamBench and IMO, and means over successful problems for
FormalQualBench. Numina reports a budget cap rather than a cost derived
from token usage. Putnam and IMO times are summed across problems;
FormalQualBench times average successes, and Humanfia’s IMO time
includes only API time. Putnam 2025 uses Numina’s statements, whereas
the PutnamBench 2025 slice uses separate formalizations. Our
FormalQualBench Opus 4.6 result is the best of four seeds (7, 6, 8, and
6 solves); the leaderboard model attribution to Opus 4.6 is inferred.
The best@6 row on PutnamBench’s 2025 slice gives the order of magnitude
a favourable seed can reach among six attempts; its cost counts
successful attempts only. We report it next to pass@1 and pass@4, and
the four FormalQualBench seeds individually, so that the spread is
visible; we draw no conclusion from the best seed alone. The cost
measure therefore changes across tables and figures: to compare with a
published number, we adopt that work’s convention, such as campaign
totals, budget caps, or cost conditional on success. Wherever our data
allow, we also report the full cost including failed attempts, and we
claim comparable or lower cost at matched models rather than uniform
cost dominance across systems.

#### Targeted completion of the last two problems.

The GPT-5.5 continuation ran eight replicas each on putnam*2013_a5 and
putnam_2021_a6 using benchmark revision b9e18f6 and Lean 4.27, obtaining
seven and one SafeVerify-accepted proofs, respectively. PutnamBench has
corrected formalizations since our original campaign, including that of
putnam_2013_a5; these corrections also allowed other systems to reach
672 solves ([Logical Intelligence, 2026](#bib.bib54); [Humanfia,
2026](#bib.bib52)). The 672 result therefore combines our original
campaign with the corrected statements. For each problem $`i`$, we
estimate parallel stopping cost as $`\sum*{j}\min(c*{ij},s*{i})`$, where
$`c*{ij}`$ is replica $`j`$’s final cost and $`s*{i}`$ the cheapest
successful replica’s cost. This adds \$5,839.36, yielding \$17.86 per
problem across 672 problems. It assumes cancellation at equal dollar
cost, not equal elapsed time. Including the full \$7,938.75 continuation
instead gives \$20.99 per problem.
