### C.6 Statistical significance and uncertainty

Many comparisons in this paper rest on a single run per configuration.
Repeating every run would multiply an already large inference cost, and
we judge single runs sufficient for the claims they support, because
most of them are existence claims: that a simple loop _can_ reach a
given score at a given cost. Since every accepted proof is formally
verified, one run establishes such a claim; for example, a single run
shows that h1 with GPT-5.5 can solve 670 of the 672 PutnamBench
problems. Where a claim requires statistical significance, we repeat
runs or resample problems and report 95% confidence intervals, as in the
tool ablation
(Figure [21](#A6.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")),
the Erdős prompt comparison
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")),
and the reflection-input costs
(Table [16](#A6.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

#### Ablation effect sizes.

Figure [21](#A6.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
summarizes both coverage and cost. Its tool comparison rewards solving
earlier: if $`S(b)`$ is the fraction solved by cost $`b`$, we summarize
the curve by $`E(B)=\frac{100}{B}\int_{0}^{B}S(b)\,db`$. Equivalently,
each problem solved at cost $`a_{i}\leq B`$ earns $`100(1-a_{i}/B)`$ and
an unsolved problem earns zero; the score averages all 100 problems. The
API-equivalent cost of a successful run is our proxy for
first-acceptance cost. We compare configurations by averaging their
score differences on the same problems. Upper boxes use the
working-file-only configuration with the detailed prompt as reference;
lower boxes use all tools with the detailed prompt.

The 95% percentile intervals use 50,000 bootstrap resamples of whole
paired problems, sharing resampling indices across configurations within
a benchmark.

For the Erdős prompt comparison in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"),
we compute 95% bootstrap intervals by resampling the observed runs with
replacement: 16 runs for the detailed-prompt reference and ten for each
other configuration. Each sampled run retains its outcomes on all six
problems. Each resample recomputes pass@$`k`$ at the \$150 per-attempt
cap, with crashes and missing results counted as unsolved.

### C.7 Proof screening

We recover AxProverBase proofs from traces’ final candidates. Removing
native_decide removes 35 accepted proofs across nine runs. Screened
counts are used in the aggregate matched-cap comparison in
Section [4](#S4 "4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving");
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
(right) retains unscreened counts. SafeVerify accepts our proofs and
rejects sorryAx, new axioms, and evaluation via native_decide.

### D.2 Misformalizations and editable answers

Kernel checking establishes a proposition, but does not establish that
it expresses the intended problem.
Table [13](#A4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ D.2 Misformalizations and editable answers ‣ Appendix D Open-Problem Proofs and Statement Corrections ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
summarizes statement defects identified in our Formal Conjectures audit
and the benchmark repairs. An editable answer creates a separate
problem: when a submission can change a definition referenced by the
target, it can make the target reflexive or vacuous. Such outputs do not
count as solutions. We fix answers or quantify witnesses satisfying the
intended mathematical constraints, and exclude exact-answer targets when
that transformation would discard the mathematical question.

The smooth four-dimensional Poincaré variant illustrates a missing
hypothesis. Its SmoothConjectureFor predicate omitted T2Space, allowing
non-Hausdorff smooth manifolds homotopy equivalent to $`\mathbb{S}^{4}`$
but not homeomorphic to it. A concurrent upstream correction adds the
Hausdorff assumption and a Lean counterexample to the old
statement ([Deicyde, 2026](#bib.bib77)).

| Target                              | Defect                                                                                                                                   | Correction or scoring decision                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Erdős 507                           | Signed triangle area and repeated vertices do not express the intended minimum nonnegative area of three distinct points.                | Proofs of the original targets do not establish the intended geometric result.                                                                        |
| Green 16                            | One natural-number answer is used for every $`N`$, although the extremal quantity depends on $`N`$.                                      | Define the extremal function of $`N`$ and state the asymptotic bound.                                                                                 |
| Erdős 566/567                       | The size Ramsey number counts edges of an arbitrary host, whereas the source asks for the ordinary Ramsey number.                        | Use the least number of vertices of a complete host.                                                                                                  |
| Lam–Litt                            | A chosen denominator can vanish at the initial point, making the cleared-denominator identity degenerate.                                | Require that denominator to be nonzero at the initial point.                                                                                          |
| Written on the Wall II, 100/160/314 | The extraction loses a complement, substitutes a cycle count for a binary indicator, or uses average distance for induced-path length.   | Restore the complement-degree norm, the $`C_{4}`$-free indicator, and the largest induced-path order, respectively.                                   |
| Open Quantum Problem 13             | Editable answers do not fix the proposed maximum number of mutually unbiased bases.                                                      | State the fixed dimension-six conjecture IsMaxMUBCount 6 3.                                                                                           |
| Other editable-answer targets       | Choosing an answer can make an equality reflexive or an asymptotic claim vacuous; choosing and refuting an answer is also uninformative. | Fix the answer or quantify a substantive witness; exclude tautological exact-answer reformulations and disable disproof mode for answer-hole targets. |

### E.1 Remaining advantages of specialized systems

Among 707 problems, two fixed-model exceptions stood out: the
group-theoretic BurnsidePrimeDegree and the density problem Erdős 125
(Appendix [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Erdős problems: individual scaling curves ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
On FormalQualBench with Opus 4.7, MerLean leads h1 by one solve with or
without the four-hour cutoff
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
MerLean proves BurnsidePrimeDegree in 3h12m with a 32-node
decomposition ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib46)); eleven h1 attempts fail
despite a combined \$6,000 and 255 hours. With Opus 4.8, we stopped our
FormalQualBench run by hand after 17 hours because of time and compute
limits
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving"));
it had not proved BurnsidePrimeDegree by iteration 19 (\$195), so that
run’s 13/23 is a lower bound. With GPT-5.6 Sol, however, h1 proves
BurnsidePrimeDegree
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
On Erdős 125, full APN reaches 50% at pass@1, basic reaches only 10% at
pass@10, and all sixteen h1 attempts end in unrecoverable Lean REPL
timeouts, an interface limitation
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Inference budgets and cost curves ‣ Appendix C Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving");
Figure [8](#A5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ E.4 Erdős problems: individual scaling curves ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving");
Appendix [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Erdős problems: individual scaling curves ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

Specialized harnesses may still reduce time to a solution, even when h1
matches their solve rate at lower cost. Numina solves twelve in less
summed time than h1 with GPT-5.2, possibly helped by faster constituent
models
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Repetition closes most remaining gaps. ‣ 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows ‣ 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
Multi-agent parallelization could further reduce elapsed time, a
capability orthogonal to h1’s simple sequential search that we discuss
in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Conclusion, limitations, and discussion ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving").

### E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus

We selected the six Erdős problem instances in Figure 3 of [Tsoukalas et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib50) for direct comparison: 12(i), 12(ii), 26, 125,
138, and 152.

AlphaProof Nexus operates on Lean files with explicitly marked editable
regions: EVOLVE-BLOCK regions contain proof code, while EVOLVE-VALUE
regions allow the agent to determine values within the statement,
including a conjecture’s truth value ([Tsoukalas et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50), Section 2 and Appendix A.2). We reconstruct our tasks
from the statements and edit boundaries in APN’s public GitHub
release,⁴⁴ 4
[https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results)
removing the proofs and withholding truth values wherever these are
marked editable. This preserves the fixed parts of each statement. We
interpret these released specifications as corresponding to the tasks
underlying APN’s reported comparison results, although the paper does
not explicitly confirm the initial files used for those experiments.

We run these experiments in an isolated environment without internet
access or access to existing solutions on the host filesystem. After
observing attempts to use the Lean REPL to explore the filesystem, we
also explicitly inform the model of this isolation to discourage such
attempts and avoid wasting inference budget
(Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection ‣ Appendix B Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).
The reflection LLM also redirects the prover away from these attempts
and toward mathematical work in the next iteration. This is part of the
effective repair loop that supports h1’s efficiency
(Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2 "The loop, not the model, decides when to stop. ‣ 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")):
carrying lessons from unproductive attempts into the next iteration
helps direct additional inference budget toward sustained progress.

We follow [Tsoukalas et al. (2026)](#bib.bib50) in reporting inference
cost conditional on success. This permits comparison with their
published per-problem results. For $`k`$ parallel attempts, we sum all
members’ costs up to the first accepted proof, including the costs of
unsuccessful members. Groups with no accepted proof contribute to the
failure rate but not to the conditional-cost mean. Thus this metric
measures the token-based cost of successful searches; it does not
measure total cost across successes and failures. APN does not report
the failed-group costs needed for this comparison.

To measure how a larger inference budget improves success at fixed
$`k`$, we vary the same per-attempt dollar allowance \$$`B`$ across
problems. Within each group, attempts stop at the first accepted proof
obtained within that allowance. For problem $`i`$, let
$`\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)`$ be the successful $`k`$-subsets of our $`n=16`$
replicas under per-attempt allowance \$$`B`$. If $`\tau_{i,G}`$ is the
first eligible proof’s active-time timestamp and $`C_{i,r}(\tau)`$ the
recorded cumulative cost of replica $`r`$, we compute

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\widehat{p}_{i,k}(B)=\frac{|\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)|}{\binom{n}{k}},\qquad\widehat{c}_{i,k}(B)=\frac{\sum_{G\in\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)}\sum_{r\in G}\min\{B,C_{i,r}(\tau_{i,G})\}}{|\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)|}.
``` |  | (1) |

Active time excludes gaps between resumed sessions. Only completed model
calls contribute cost, using the specified token prices. We average both
coordinates equally over the same fixed problem set $`I`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\overline{c}_{I,k}(B)=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}\widehat{c}_{i,k}(B),\qquad\overline{p}_{I,k}(B)=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}\widehat{p}_{i,k}(B).
``` |  | (2) |

The plotted frontier retains nondominated cost–success points, using
only allowances for which every problem in $`I`$ has an observed success
and hence a defined conditional cost. APN basic’s pass@$`k`$ rates are
its published grouped-run estimates; our rates use the subset estimator
over recorded replicas. APN full reports ten attempts per problem. The
published APN coordinates receive the same equal problem weights. This
differs from pooling successful attempts, which would give easier
problems more weight. The overlapping subsets do not provide independent
observations for estimating uncertainty, and APN does not report
uncertainty for this aggregate.

The cost–success frontier in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
compares the five problems with observed successes in all three systems:
12(i), 12(ii), 138, 152, and 26. This subset does not include Erdős 125:
all h1 attempts encounter Lean timeouts, leaving its success-conditional
cost undefined. Across the full six-problem set, including these
failures, h1 achieves 68.75% at pass@1, close to APN full’s 71.67%, and
surpasses APN full’s pass@1 success rate with 79.73% at pass@3
(Table [15](#A5.T15 "Table 15 ‣ E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")).

| $`k`$ | h1 (%) | APN basic (%) | APN full (%) |
|-------|--------|---------------|--------------|
| 1     | 68.75  | 35.67         | 71.67        |
| 3     | 79.73  | 63.36         | –            |
| 6     | 82.90  | 76.14         | –            |
| 10    | 83.33  | 81.82         | –            |

Table 15: Success rates across all six Erdős problems. Each entry is
$`100/6`$ times the sum of the six per-problem pass@$`k`$ estimates,
giving every problem equal weight. For h1, each estimate is
$`1-\binom{16-c_{i}}{k}/\binom{16}{k}`$, where $`c_{i}`$ is the number
of accepted replicas; all errors count as failures, including all 16 on
problem 125. APN columns average the published per-problem rates with
the same weights. These are terminal outcomes, not matched-budget
estimates.

#### Counting unsuccessful searches.

To compare compute allocation within h1, we also report mean spend over
all groups, including those with no accepted proof. Let
$`\mathcal{G}_{i,k}`$ be all $`k`$-subsets of the $`n=16`$ replicas, and
let $`C_{i,r}(\infty)`$ denote a replica’s recorded terminal cost. The
unconditional estimate is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{u}_{i,k}(B)=\frac{1}{\binom{n}{k}}\left[\sum_{G\in\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)}\sum_{r\in G}\min\{B,C_{i,r}(\tau_{i,G})\}+\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{i,k}(B)}\sum_{r\in G}\min\{B,C_{i,r}(\infty)\}\right].
``` |  | (3) |

We use the same recorded attempts, token prices, dollar caps, and
first-proof cancellation rule as in
Equation [1](#A5.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ E.6 Comparing success and cost with AlphaProof Nexus ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving");
only the averaging includes unsuccessful groups. Each problem receives
equal weight. Conditioning on success selects different groups as $`k`$
changes, so the conditional metric alone does not describe the full
spending trade-off. It does not mathematically prevent repetition from
dominating a pass@1 operating point: a quick proof in one replica can
cancel expensive searches in the others. We omit APN from the
unconditional plots because its failed-group costs are unavailable.

For a hypothetical example, suppose independent attempts spend at the
same constant rate and solve at \$1 with probability $`0.8`$, solve at
\$100 with probability $`0.1`$, or fail at \$100 with probability
$`0.1`$. Pass@1 succeeds with probability $`0.9`$ at conditional mean
cost $`(0.8\times 1+0.1\times 100)/0.9=\$12`$. Two parallel attempts,
cancelled at the first proof, succeed with probability $`0.99`$ at
conditional mean cost $`(0.96\times 2+0.03\times 200)/0.99=\$8`$: a
quick success occurs with probability $`0.96`$, and a success without a
quick one with probability $`0.03`$. This establishes dominance of one
operating point, not of the entire pass@1 curve.

endpoints. Leanstral costs are API-equivalent estimates using a measured
65% average cache rate at maximum context length.

### E.8 Additional comparisons with AxProverBase and analysis of failed attempts

Figure 16: h1 overtakes AxProverBase as the budget grows across the six
settings in Figure . AxProverBase is shown both before and after
screening out proofs using native_decide; overlapping lines indicate no
screened solves. All h1 solves pass external validation.

Figure 17: Cost per problem by token type, PutnamBench subset, nine
model settings under AxProverBase (AxP) and h1. Bars average costs
across solved and unsolved problems. Percentages show output tokens’
share of total cost.

With Gemini 3 Flash on the PutnamBench subset, h1 solves all 18 problems
solved by AxProverBase and 51 additional problems. On those 51, mean
proposer-call counts are 287 for AxProverBase and 275 for h1. Mean
output per problem, including reflection, is 5.97M versus 0.628M tokens;
mean input is 4.24M versus 23.13M, respectively. The fraction of input
served from cache is 0.04% for AxProverBase and 78.8% for h1.
AxProverBase regenerates a complete candidate after feedback; h1 retains
the file and makes local edits. These observations connect the
token-cost difference to how the systems preserve work, without
isolating it from their other design differences.

Figure 18: PutnamBench subset solve rates for h1 and AxProverBase as the
budget increases. h1 with Opus 4.5 solves 61 problems at the \$20
per-problem cap.

Figure 19: Bad imports consume proof-checking attempts. The fraction of
failed builds whose first Lean error is a bad import is 42.2% for
AxProverBase with Gemini 3 Flash and 0.6% with Opus 4.5; dashed lines
show the paper’s reported 56% and 0.4%. h1 seeds the working file with
import Mathlib and records no such failures.

For example, on putnam_1972_b4, AxProverBase uses tokens equivalent to
\$20.01 over 287 builds, including 175 bad-import and 84 syntax
failures. h1 solves it at an API-equivalent cost of \$0.15 with 20 local
edits, three REPL tests, and one submission. Across the 51 h1-only
solves, AxProverBase performs 13,446 reflections and h1 performs 316,
while the systems differ in whether they regenerate or edit the working
file.

### E.9 Additional comparisons with Claude Code and analysis of failed attempts

With the same Claude model, native Claude Code (with its built-in shell
and file tools), Claude Code with our prompt and Lean tools through MCP
(which replace the built-in tools), and h1 solve 81/95/99 PutnamBench
subset problems and 63/73/83 FATE-X problems, respectively
(Figures [5](#A5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ E.1 Remaining advantages of specialized systems ‣ Appendix E Additional Results for Section 3 ‣ h1 : A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving")
and , right). The tools expose Lean feedback and SafeVerify rejection
within the session; h1 additionally enforces validation and another
repair round after rejection.

Relative to native Claude Code, exposing final-proof validation
addresses a frequent failure mode. Of 30 problems solved by h1 where
native Claude Code stops normally without an accepted proof, 28 end with
an artifact rejected by SafeVerify. Adding our Lean tools to Claude Code
solves 20 of these problems. h1 uses multiple rounds on 21 of the 30.

Relative to Claude Code with MCP tools, h1 additionally controls how
execution continues after failures. On FATE-X problem 19, Claude Code
with our tools resubmits an unchanged file 170 times, whereas h1 edits
after each of 17 negative outcomes and succeeds.

The MCP integration also leaves API-call retries under Claude Code’s
control. Some Claude Code runs fail through API-call errors and repeated
timeouts. We took care to give these baselines their strongest showing:
we restarted affected runs from scratch, and reran configurations whose
wall-time limit was binding with a larger allowance. Exposing Lean tools
through MCP does not give the experimenter the same control over Claude
Code’s internal retries and failure handling as implementing the harness
directly. In h1, these policies are explicit: transient connection
failures can retry the same call, while verifier failures return
feedback for further edits.

## Appendix F Tool, Prompt, and Reflection Ablations

Figure 21: Tools provide overlapping benefits. Individual search tools
or the REPL recover most of the full tool set’s gains; removing any

Figure 22: The detailed prompt improves solve rates on both ablation
settings. Gemini 3 Flash on the PutnamBench subset (\$20 per problem)

The reflection-input ablation varies the context supplied to the
reflection LLM, independently of its system prompt. With the transcript,
it receives the latest attempt’s reasoning, final code, verifier
feedback, and interaction transcript. The distilled final attempt
consists of the multi-turn LLM’s account of its latest attempt, the
final Lean code, the verifier feedback, and the previous reflection
summary; the sequence of intermediate model turns, tool calls, and tool
results is omitted.

respectively, including prover and reflection LLM calls; each arm
contains 100 problems and one run.
````
